sentences.text: The bones of Qinornis display uniquely primitive characteristics for its age, leading researchers to debate whether it was a juvenile modern bird or an adult non-neornithine bird that survived the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.
Unusually for a bird of its recent age, the foot bones of Qinornis are not completely fused.
Qinornis is known from a single fossil specimen found in the Fangou Formation in Luonan County, China.
The genus Qinornis was described by Xue in 1995.
The type species of the genus Qinornis is Qinornis paleocenica.
Qinornis belongs to the parent group Ornithurae.
Qinornis lived during the early to mid-Paleocene epoch, approximately 61 million years ago.
The time range for Qinornis is from 66 to 61.66 million years ago.
Mayr argued in 2007 that the Qinornis specimen was an adult because the distal tarsalia were fused with the metatarsalia and lacked the blurred surfaces typical of growing juvenile neornithine birds.

Longrich and colleagues (2011) questioned Mayr's conclusion, suggesting the bones might belong to a juvenile, while also noting it was not impossible that some archaic birds persisted beyond the Cretaceous period.
